label: Infectious Disease
blurb: Antibacterials, antivirals, antifungals, antiparasitics, HIV and TB therapy

drugs.name: Penicillin G
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal against susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative cocci
drugs.treatmentUsage: Syphilis (drug of choice), group A and B streptococcal infections, Neisseria meningitidis meningitis, Clostridium perfringens, actinomycosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits transpeptidase cross-linking of peptidoglycan, while also activating autolysins that degrade the cell wall.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis, hemolytic anemia, interstitial nephritis, seizures at very high doses, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in syphilis
drugs.contraindications: Known penicillin anaphylaxis; beta-lactamase-producing organisms are intrinsically resistant
drugs.tooltip: Still the drug of choice for syphilis at every stage, with no documented Treponema resistance. Penicillin-allergic pregnant patients must be desensitized rather than given an alternative.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal with extended gram-negative coverage
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute otitis media (first-line), streptococcal pharyngitis, sinusitis, Helicobacter pylori eradication, Lyme disease, endocarditis prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits transpeptidase-mediated peptidoglycan cross-linking; the amino group improves penetration through gram-negative porin channels.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea, rash, hypersensitivity, pseudomembranous colitis, characteristic maculopapular rash if given during Epstein-Barr virus infection
drugs.contraindications: Penicillin allergy; ineffective against beta-lactamase producers unless combined with clavulanate
drugs.tooltip: Classic vignette: a teenager with sore throat gets amoxicillin and develops a diffuse maculopapular rash — that indicates infectious mononucleosis, not a true penicillin allergy.

drugs.name: Piperacillin / Tazobactam
drugs.primaryEffect: Broad-spectrum bactericidal activity including Pseudomonas and anaerobes
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hospital-acquired pneumonia, intra-abdominal infection, febrile neutropenia, complicated skin and soft tissue infection, sepsis of unknown source
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Piperacillin inhibits cell wall cross-linking while tazobactam irreversibly inhibits many beta-lactamases, protecting piperacillin from degradation.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea, hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile colitis, thrombocytopenia, hypokalemia, nephrotoxicity when combined with vancomycin
drugs.contraindications: Penicillin anaphylaxis; ineffective against MRSA, atypicals, and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers
drugs.tooltip: The empiric workhorse for hospital sepsis. It covers Pseudomonas and anaerobes but not MRSA, so vancomycin is added. The combination carries a well-known nephrotoxicity signal.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.primaryEffect: Broad gram-negative coverage with excellent CNS penetration
drugs.treatmentUsage: Bacterial meningitis, gonorrhea, community-acquired pneumonia, pyelonephritis, Lyme disease with neurologic involvement, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds penicillin-binding proteins to block peptidoglycan cross-linking; its beta-lactam ring is more resistant to many beta-lactamases than earlier cephalosporins.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea, hypersensitivity, biliary sludging and pseudocholelithiasis, kernicterus in neonates, Clostridioides difficile colitis
drugs.contraindications: Neonates especially with hyperbilirubinemia, concurrent calcium-containing intravenous solutions in neonates, severe cephalosporin allergy
drugs.tooltip: Crosses the blood-brain barrier well, making it the meningitis backbone. Avoided in neonates because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and can cause kernicterus.

drugs.name: Cefazolin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal against skin flora and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus
drugs.treatmentUsage: Surgical prophylaxis, methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, cellulitis, osteomyelitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins and blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypersensitivity, diarrhea, phlebitis, rare seizures at high dose in renal failure, Clostridioides difficile colitis
drugs.contraindications: Severe cephalosporin or penicillin anaphylaxis; does not cross into the CNS and does not cover MRSA or enterococci
drugs.tooltip: The standard preoperative prophylaxis given within one hour of incision. First-generation cephalosporins cover PEcK: Proteus, E. coli, and Klebsiella, plus gram-positive cocci.

drugs.name: Cefepime
drugs.primaryEffect: Broad gram-negative coverage including Pseudomonas with retained gram-positive activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Febrile neutropenia, hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, complicated urinary tract infection, Pseudomonas infections
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Zwitterionic structure allows rapid penetration of gram-negative porins and gives high stability against AmpC beta-lactamases while binding penicillin-binding proteins.
drugs.sideEffects: Neurotoxicity with encephalopathy, myoclonus, and nonconvulsive status epilepticus especially in renal impairment; diarrhea; hypersensitivity
drugs.contraindications: Severe cephalosporin allergy; requires renal dose adjustment to avoid neurotoxicity
drugs.tooltip: Standard empiric monotherapy for febrile neutropenia. Cefepime neurotoxicity is a classic ICU scenario: a confused patient with myoclonus and renal failure on high-dose cefepime.

drugs.name: Ceftaroline
drugs.primaryEffect: Cephalosporin with activity against MRSA
drugs.treatmentUsage: Complicated skin and soft tissue infection and community-acquired pneumonia caused by MRSA
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Uniquely binds penicillin-binding protein 2a, the altered PBP encoded by mecA that confers methicillin resistance, allowing cell wall inhibition in MRSA.
drugs.sideEffects: Rash, diarrhea, nausea, neutropenia with prolonged use, direct Coombs positivity, hypersensitivity
drugs.contraindications: Severe cephalosporin allergy; lacks Pseudomonas coverage
drugs.tooltip: The only beta-lactam that treats MRSA, because it binds PBP2a which all other beta-lactams cannot. Note it does not cover Pseudomonas despite being fifth generation.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.primaryEffect: Extremely broad bactericidal activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers, polymicrobial intra-abdominal sepsis, meningitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds penicillin-binding proteins with high affinity and resists most beta-lactamases including extended-spectrum enzymes, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea, seizures (less than imipenem), hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile colitis, reduced valproate levels
drugs.contraindications: Carbapenem hypersensitivity; concurrent valproate because levels fall precipitously and seizures result
drugs.tooltip: The broadest beta-lactam class, covering gram-positives, gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, and anaerobes — but not MRSA, VRE, or atypicals. Imipenem needs cilastatin to block renal dehydropeptidase.

drugs.name: Aztreonam
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal against aerobic gram-negative organisms only
drugs.treatmentUsage: Gram-negative infections including Pseudomonas in patients with severe penicillin allergy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Monocyclic beta-lactam that binds penicillin-binding protein 3 of aerobic gram-negative bacteria, with no activity against gram-positives or anaerobes.
drugs.sideEffects: Rash, diarrhea, elevated transaminases, phlebitis; very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to aztreonam itself; no gram-positive or anaerobic coverage means it cannot be used empirically alone
drugs.tooltip: The answer when a patient has true penicillin anaphylaxis but needs gram-negative coverage, because there is essentially no cross-reactivity except with ceftazidime, which shares a side chain.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal against gram-positive organisms including MRSA
drugs.treatmentUsage: MRSA infections, methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci, ampicillin-resistant enterococci, oral therapy for Clostridioides difficile colitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, sterically preventing transglycosylation and transpeptidation of the cell wall.
drugs.sideEffects: Vancomycin infusion reaction with flushing of the upper body, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neutropenia, DRESS syndrome, thrombocytopenia
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; requires level monitoring and renal dose adjustment; oral form only for Clostridioides difficile since it is not absorbed
drugs.tooltip: The infusion reaction is direct mast cell degranulation from rapid infusion, not IgE allergy, and it resolves with slower administration. Resistance in VRE comes from D-ala-D-lac substitution.

drugs.name: Daptomycin
drugs.primaryEffect: Rapid bactericidal killing of gram-positive organisms
drugs.treatmentUsage: MRSA bacteremia and right-sided endocarditis, vancomycin-resistant enterococci, complicated skin and soft tissue infection
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inserts its lipid tail into the gram-positive cell membrane in a calcium-dependent manner, forming pores that cause rapid membrane depolarization and potassium efflux.
drugs.sideEffects: Myopathy with elevated creatine kinase requiring weekly monitoring, rhabdomyolysis, eosinophilic pneumonia, peripheral neuropathy
drugs.contraindications: Pneumonia of any cause because pulmonary surfactant inactivates it; caution with concurrent statins
drugs.tooltip: Never use daptomycin for pneumonia — surfactant binds and inactivates it. Weekly creatine kinase monitoring is required, and statins are usually held during therapy.

drugs.name: Linezolid
drugs.primaryEffect: Bacteriostatic inhibition of gram-positive protein synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci, MRSA pneumonia and skin infection, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the 23S ribosomal RNA of the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the 70S initiation complex, blocking protein synthesis at the very first step.
drugs.sideEffects: Reversible myelosuppression especially thrombocytopenia, peripheral and optic neuropathy with prolonged use, serotonin syndrome, lactic acidosis
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent MAO inhibitors; caution with SSRIs and other serotonergic drugs; tyramine-rich foods
drugs.tooltip: It is a weak MAO inhibitor, which is the tested interaction: linezolid plus an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome. Excellent oral bioavailability means no dose change from IV to oral.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bacteriostatic against atypical and respiratory pathogens
drugs.treatmentUsage: Community-acquired pneumonia, atypical pneumonia from Mycoplasma or Legionella, chlamydia, pertussis, Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation of the growing peptide chain, halting protein synthesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Gastrointestinal upset from motilin receptor agonism, QT prolongation, cholestatic hepatitis, hearing loss with prolonged use
drugs.contraindications: Known long QT syndrome, concurrent QT-prolonging drugs, history of cholestatic jaundice with macrolides
drugs.tooltip: Azithromycin has minimal CYP3A4 inhibition unlike erythromycin and clarithromycin, which is why it is preferred when drug interactions matter. QT prolongation remains a class effect.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.primaryEffect: Bacteriostatic with broad atypical and intracellular coverage
drugs.treatmentUsage: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, chlamydia, community-acquired MRSA skin infection, acne, malaria prophylaxis, atypical pneumonia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the acceptor site, preventing peptide chain elongation.
drugs.sideEffects: Photosensitivity, esophagitis if taken without water, gastrointestinal upset, tooth discoloration and impaired bone growth in children under eight, benign intracranial hypertension
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, children under age eight, concurrent divalent cations such as calcium, iron, magnesium, or antacids which chelate the drug
drugs.tooltip: The drug of choice for Rocky Mountain spotted fever even in children, because the disease is more dangerous than the tooth staining. Take with a full glass of water sitting upright to avoid esophagitis.

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.primaryEffect: Concentration-dependent bactericidal killing of aerobic gram-negatives
drugs.treatmentUsage: Serious gram-negative infections, synergy with beta-lactams for enterococcal and staphylococcal endocarditis, bowel surgery prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and premature termination; uptake requires oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobes are intrinsically resistant.
drugs.sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity with acute tubular necrosis, irreversible ototoxicity and vestibular toxicity, neuromuscular blockade, teratogenicity
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, myasthenia gravis, concurrent loop diuretics or vancomycin which compound toxicity, anaerobic infections
drugs.tooltip: Once-daily extended-interval dosing exploits concentration-dependent killing and the post-antibiotic effect while reducing nephrotoxicity. Aminoglycosides are ineffective in abscesses because of the low-oxygen environment.

drugs.name: Levofloxacin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal with broad gram-negative and respiratory coverage
drugs.treatmentUsage: Community-acquired pneumonia, complicated urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal infection, anthrax, tuberculosis as second-line
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing supercoiling relief and religation during bacterial DNA replication.
drugs.sideEffects: Tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation, CNS effects including confusion and seizures, aortic aneurysm and dissection, Clostridioides difficile colitis, dysglycemia
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, children and adolescents when alternatives exist, myasthenia gravis, concurrent divalent cations, history of tendon disorders
drugs.tooltip: Multiple boxed warnings restrict fluoroquinolones to situations without alternatives. Tendon rupture risk is highest in the Achilles tendon, in patients over 60, and with concurrent corticosteroids.

drugs.name: Ciprofloxacin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal with strong gram-negative and Pseudomonas activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Complicated urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis, traveler's diarrhea, typhoid fever, Pseudomonas infection, anthrax prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA supercoiling and causing double-strand breaks during replication.
drugs.sideEffects: Tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation, CNS toxicity, Clostridioides difficile colitis, aortic dissection, theophylline toxicity via CYP1A2 inhibition
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, pediatric use when alternatives exist, myasthenia gravis, concurrent tizanidine, divalent cation co-administration
drugs.tooltip: The best oral anti-Pseudomonal agent. It inhibits CYP1A2, which raises theophylline and caffeine levels — a classic interaction question producing seizures or arrhythmias.

drugs.name: Trimethoprim / Sulfamethoxazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Sequential blockade of bacterial folate synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, community-acquired MRSA, toxoplasmosis prophylaxis, Nocardia, Listeria
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, sequentially blocking two steps in bacterial tetrahydrofolate synthesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hyperkalemia, elevated creatinine without true renal injury, megaloblastic anemia, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, kernicterus in neonates
drugs.contraindications: Sulfa allergy, pregnancy near term, G6PD deficiency, folate deficiency, severe renal impairment, concurrent methotrexate
drugs.tooltip: Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel, which explains both the hyperkalemia and the rise in creatinine from blocked tubular secretion without actual kidney injury.

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal against anaerobes and antiprotozoal activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Anaerobic infections, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, Clostridioides difficile colitis, Helicobacter pylori regimens
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Reduced by anaerobic organisms into cytotoxic free radical intermediates that damage DNA, which requires the low-redox environment found only in anaerobes and protozoa.
drugs.sideEffects: Metallic taste, nausea, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use, seizures, dark urine
drugs.contraindications: Alcohol use during and for three days after therapy, first trimester of pregnancy, concurrent disulfiram
drugs.tooltip: The disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol is the most tested fact. Selectivity for anaerobes comes from requiring a low-redox environment to activate the drug into DNA-damaging radicals.

drugs.name: Clindamycin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bacteriostatic against gram-positives and anaerobes above the diaphragm
drugs.treatmentUsage: Anaerobic infections above the diaphragm such as lung abscess and aspiration pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock as a toxin suppressor, dental prophylaxis in penicillin allergy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit at the same site as macrolides and blocks peptide bond formation and translocation, also suppressing bacterial exotoxin production.
drugs.sideEffects: Clostridioides difficile colitis (highest risk of any antibiotic), diarrhea, rash, metallic taste, hepatotoxicity
drugs.contraindications: History of Clostridioides difficile infection, hypersensitivity; does not cover gram-negatives
drugs.tooltip: The classic C. difficile antibiotic. In necrotizing fasciitis it is added to a beta-lactam specifically because it shuts off ribosomal toxin production, an effect penicillin lacks in high inoculum.

drugs.name: Nitrofurantoin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal concentration achieved only in urine
drugs.treatmentUsage: Uncomplicated cystitis including in pregnancy; long-term urinary tract infection prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Reduced by bacterial nitroreductases into reactive intermediates that damage ribosomal proteins, DNA, and multiple metabolic enzymes simultaneously.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, brown urine discoloration, acute and chronic pulmonary reactions with fibrosis, peripheral neuropathy, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, hepatotoxicity
drugs.contraindications: Creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min because urinary levels become inadequate, pyelonephritis, G6PD deficiency, pregnancy at term
drugs.tooltip: Only concentrates in urine, so it treats cystitis but never pyelonephritis or systemic infection. Resistance remains remarkably rare after decades of use because of its multiple simultaneous targets.

drugs.name: Isoniazid
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal against replicating Mycobacterium tuberculosis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Active tuberculosis as part of RIPE therapy; latent tuberculosis infection treatment
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG, then inhibits InhA to block synthesis of mycolic acids essential to the mycobacterial cell wall.
drugs.sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy from pyridoxine depletion, drug-induced lupus, sideroblastic anemia, CYP450 inhibition, seizures in overdose
drugs.contraindications: Acute liver disease, prior isoniazid hepatitis; requires pyridoxine supplementation
drugs.tooltip: Always give vitamin B6 with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy. Slow acetylators are at higher risk for neuropathy and lupus; fast acetylators at higher risk of hepatotoxicity.

drugs.name: Rifampin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bactericidal inhibition of bacterial RNA synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae prophylaxis, prosthetic device staphylococcal infections, leprosy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and blocks initiation of transcription.
drugs.sideEffects: Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, and contact lenses; hepatotoxicity; flu-like syndrome; thrombocytopenia; potent CYP450 induction
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent protease inhibitors and many other CYP3A4 substrates; caution in hepatic impairment
drugs.tooltip: The most potent CYP450 inducer in clinical medicine, causing failure of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and HIV protease inhibitors. Orange body fluids are harmless but alarming to patients.

drugs.name: Pyrazinamide
drugs.primaryEffect: Kills mycobacteria in the acidic environment of macrophages
drugs.treatmentUsage: Tuberculosis during the first two months of intensive-phase therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Converted by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase into pyrazinoic acid, which disrupts membrane transport and energy metabolism most effectively at the acidic pH inside phagolysosomes.
drugs.sideEffects: Hyperuricemia and gout flares, hepatotoxicity, arthralgias, photosensitivity, gastrointestinal upset
drugs.contraindications: Acute gout, severe hepatic disease, pregnancy in some guidelines
drugs.tooltip: The reason tuberculosis therapy could be shortened to six months, because it kills semi-dormant intracellular organisms. Hyperuricemia and gout flares are the signature adverse effect.

drugs.name: Ethambutol
drugs.primaryEffect: Bacteriostatic inhibition of mycobacterial cell wall assembly
drugs.treatmentUsage: Tuberculosis intensive-phase therapy; Mycobacterium avium complex infection
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits arabinosyl transferase, blocking polymerization of arabinogalactan required to anchor mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall.
drugs.sideEffects: Optic neuritis with decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness, peripheral neuropathy, hyperuricemia, rash
drugs.contraindications: Preexisting optic neuritis, young children who cannot report visual changes, severe renal impairment without dose adjustment
drugs.tooltip: Ethambutol affects the Eyes: dose-dependent optic neuritis causing red-green color discrimination loss. Baseline and monthly visual acuity and color vision testing are required.

drugs.name: Acyclovir
drugs.primaryEffect: Inhibits replication of herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses
drugs.treatmentUsage: Genital and orolabial herpes, herpes encephalitis, varicella, herpes zoster, suppression of recurrent HSV
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Monophosphorylated selectively by viral thymidine kinase, then converted by host kinases to acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates the growing DNA chain.
drugs.sideEffects: Crystalline nephropathy with inadequate hydration, neurotoxicity with confusion and tremor, nausea, phlebitis
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; requires adequate hydration and renal dose adjustment
drugs.tooltip: Selectivity comes entirely from the first phosphorylation requiring viral thymidine kinase, so uninfected cells are spared. Thymidine kinase mutation is the main resistance mechanism, treated with foscarnet.

drugs.name: Ganciclovir
drugs.primaryEffect: Inhibits cytomegalovirus DNA replication
drugs.treatmentUsage: Cytomegalovirus retinitis, colitis, and pneumonitis in immunocompromised patients; CMV prophylaxis after transplant
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Phosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase then by cellular kinases to the triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates chain elongation.
drugs.sideEffects: Severe myelosuppression with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, nephrotoxicity, seizures, carcinogenicity and teratogenicity
drugs.contraindications: Absolute neutrophil count below 500 or platelets below 25,000, pregnancy
drugs.tooltip: Far more myelosuppressive than acyclovir, which limits its use. Valganciclovir is the oral prodrug used for prophylaxis. Resistance from UL97 mutation is treated with foscarnet or cidofovir.

drugs.name: Oseltamivir
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents release of influenza virions from infected cells
drugs.treatmentUsage: Treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A and B, most effective within 48 hours of symptom onset
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits viral neuraminidase, the enzyme that cleaves sialic acid to release progeny virions from the host cell surface, so new virus remains bound and cannot spread.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea and vomiting, headache, rare neuropsychiatric events in adolescents including delirium
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; requires renal dose adjustment
drugs.tooltip: Shortens illness by about one day if started within 48 hours; the real value is in high-risk and hospitalized patients. Hemagglutinin lets virus in, neuraminidase lets it out.

drugs.name: Tenofovir
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks reverse transcription of HIV and hepatitis B
drugs.treatmentUsage: HIV treatment as part of combination therapy, HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, chronic hepatitis B
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A nucleotide analog already bearing one phosphate that requires only two further phosphorylations; it competitively inhibits reverse transcriptase and terminates the DNA chain.
drugs.sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity with proximal tubulopathy and Fanconi syndrome, decreased bone mineral density, lactic acidosis; the alafenamide formulation greatly reduces both
drugs.contraindications: Severe renal impairment for the disoproxil formulation; hepatitis B flare on discontinuation
drugs.tooltip: The backbone of most HIV regimens and of pre-exposure prophylaxis. Tenofovir alafenamide delivers drug intracellularly at far lower plasma levels, sharply reducing renal and bone toxicity.

drugs.name: Emtricitabine
drugs.primaryEffect: Terminates HIV proviral DNA synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: HIV combination therapy and pre-exposure prophylaxis, almost always paired with tenofovir; also active against hepatitis B
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Cytidine analog phosphorylated intracellularly to the triphosphate, which competes with deoxycytidine triphosphate and terminates the DNA chain after incorporation.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, nausea, skin hyperpigmentation especially of palms and soles, lactic acidosis, hepatitis B flare on discontinuation
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; requires renal dose adjustment; do not stop abruptly in hepatitis B coinfection
drugs.tooltip: Very well tolerated and paired with tenofovir in nearly every first-line regimen and in PrEP. Palmar and plantar hyperpigmentation is a distinctive if uncommon finding.

drugs.name: Dolutegravir
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents HIV proviral DNA from integrating into host DNA
drugs.treatmentUsage: First-line HIV therapy in combination with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Chelates magnesium ions in the integrase active site, blocking the strand transfer step that inserts viral DNA into the host genome.
drugs.sideEffects: Insomnia, headache, weight gain, small increase in serum creatinine from blocked tubular secretion without true renal injury, rare hepatotoxicity and hypersensitivity
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent dofetilide; separate dosing from polyvalent cation antacids and supplements which chelate the drug
drugs.tooltip: Integrase inhibitors are first-line because of high potency, few interactions, and a high barrier to resistance. The creatinine rise is from blocked tubular secretion, not nephrotoxicity.

drugs.name: Efavirenz
drugs.primaryEffect: Directly inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase
drugs.treatmentUsage: HIV combination therapy, historically a first-line agent, now largely replaced by integrase inhibitors
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds a hydrophobic allosteric pocket adjacent to the reverse transcriptase active site, causing a conformational change that inactivates the enzyme without requiring phosphorylation.
drugs.sideEffects: Vivid dreams, nightmares, dizziness, and mood changes; rash; hyperlipidemia; false-positive cannabinoid screens; teratogenicity concerns historically
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent drugs heavily dependent on CYP3A4; caution with psychiatric illness
drugs.tooltip: Central nervous system side effects — vivid dreams and dizziness — usually appear in the first weeks and improve. Dosing at bedtime on an empty stomach minimizes them.

drugs.name: Ritonavir
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks HIV protease and boosts levels of other antivirals
drugs.treatmentUsage: Pharmacokinetic booster for other protease inhibitors and for nirmatrelvir in COVID-19; historically HIV therapy at full dose
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits HIV-1 protease, preventing cleavage of gag-pol polyprotein into functional proteins so immature noninfectious virions are produced; it also potently inhibits CYP3A4.
drugs.sideEffects: Gastrointestinal intolerance, hyperlipidemia, insulin resistance, lipodystrophy with fat redistribution, hepatotoxicity, extensive drug interactions
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent drugs with narrow therapeutic index metabolized by CYP3A4 such as ergots, midazolam, simvastatin, and rifampin
drugs.tooltip: Used today almost entirely for its CYP3A4 inhibition rather than antiviral effect — a rare case where a side effect became the indication. Protease inhibitors end in -navir and cause lipodystrophy.

drugs.name: Sofosbuvir
drugs.primaryEffect: Cures chronic hepatitis C infection
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic hepatitis C, combined with an NS5A inhibitor such as velpatasvir or ledipasvir
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Uridine nucleotide analog prodrug that, once triphosphorylated in hepatocytes, is incorporated by the NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and terminates viral RNA synthesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Fatigue, headache, nausea, bradycardia when combined with amiodarone, hepatitis B reactivation
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent amiodarone because of symptomatic bradycardia; concurrent potent P-glycoprotein inducers such as rifampin or St. John's wort
drugs.tooltip: Direct-acting antivirals cure over 95 percent of hepatitis C in 8 to 12 oral weeks, replacing interferon entirely. Screen for hepatitis B first because treatment can trigger reactivation.

drugs.name: Fluconazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Fungistatic disruption of fungal membrane synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Candidiasis including esophageal and vaginal, cryptococcal meningitis maintenance therapy, coccidioidomycosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol and destabilizing the fungal cell membrane.
drugs.sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, nausea, rash, teratogenicity at high doses, numerous CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 interactions
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy at high doses, concurrent QT-prolonging drugs, coadministration with cisapride or pimozide
drugs.tooltip: Excellent CSF and urine penetration, which distinguishes it from other azoles. Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant and Candida glabrata often is, so speciation matters.

drugs.name: Amphotericin B
drugs.primaryEffect: Fungicidal disruption of the fungal cell membrane
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe systemic mycoses including cryptococcal meningitis induction, mucormycosis, severe histoplasmosis and blastomycosis, visceral leishmaniasis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane and forms transmembrane pores that allow potassium and other ions to leak out, causing cell death.
drugs.sideEffects: Infusion reactions with fever and rigors, nephrotoxicity with potassium and magnesium wasting, renal tubular acidosis, anemia, phlebitis
drugs.contraindications: Significant renal impairment; requires aggressive sodium loading and electrolyte repletion; liposomal formulations reduce toxicity
drugs.tooltip: Nicknamed amphoterrible for shake-and-bake infusion reactions and nephrotoxicity. Pretreatment with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine plus saline loading reduces toxicity; liposomal forms reduce it further.

drugs.name: Caspofungin
drugs.primaryEffect: Fungicidal against Candida through cell wall disruption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Invasive candidiasis and candidemia (first-line), esophageal candidiasis, salvage therapy for invasive aspergillosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Noncompetitively inhibits beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, preventing synthesis of a cell wall polysaccharide unique to fungi and absent in humans.
drugs.sideEffects: Infusion-related histamine reactions, elevated transaminases, hypokalemia, fever; overall very well tolerated
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; not active against Cryptococcus which lacks substantial beta-glucan, nor Mucorales
drugs.tooltip: Echinocandins target a structure humans do not have, so they are remarkably safe. They are first-line for candidemia but useless against Cryptococcus, whose capsule structure differs.

drugs.name: Voriconazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Broad antifungal activity including molds
drugs.treatmentUsage: Invasive aspergillosis (drug of choice), Scedosporium and Fusarium infections, refractory candidiasis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits fungal 14-alpha-demethylase with a broader spectrum than fluconazole, halting ergosterol synthesis and disrupting membrane integrity.
drugs.sideEffects: Transient visual disturbances with bright light and color changes, hallucinations, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity with long-term squamous cell carcinoma risk, QT prolongation, periostitis
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent rifampin, carbamazepine, ergots, sirolimus, or pimozide; severe hepatic impairment
drugs.tooltip: The drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis. The reversible visual disturbance in the first days of therapy is a striking and heavily tested adverse effect. Requires therapeutic drug monitoring.

drugs.name: Terbinafine
drugs.primaryEffect: Fungicidal against dermatophytes
drugs.treatmentUsage: Onychomycosis, tinea capitis, tinea pedis and other dermatophyte infections
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis at an earlier step than azoles and causing toxic squalene accumulation within the fungus.
drugs.sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity, taste and smell disturbance sometimes permanent, headache, rash, rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome, lupus-like reaction
drugs.contraindications: Chronic or active liver disease; requires baseline liver function testing
drugs.tooltip: It accumulates in keratin, which is why it works for nails but requires months of therapy. Loss of taste is a distinctive adverse effect that can persist after stopping the drug.

drugs.name: Chloroquine
drugs.primaryEffect: Kills blood-stage malaria parasites
drugs.treatmentUsage: Malaria treatment and prophylaxis in chloroquine-sensitive regions; extraintestinal amebiasis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Concentrates in the parasite food vacuole and inhibits heme polymerase, preventing detoxification of heme into hemozoin so free heme accumulates and kills the parasite.
drugs.sideEffects: Retinopathy with long-term use, pruritus, gastrointestinal upset, QT prolongation, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, cardiomyopathy
drugs.contraindications: Preexisting retinopathy, chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum regions, G6PD deficiency with caution
drugs.tooltip: Widespread resistance limits it to a few regions. It kills only blood stages, so Plasmodium vivax and ovale also require primaquine to eradicate dormant hepatic hypnozoites.

drugs.name: Primaquine
drugs.primaryEffect: Eradicates dormant liver-stage malaria parasites
drugs.treatmentUsage: Radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and ovale by clearing hypnozoites; malaria prophylaxis; Pneumocystis with clindamycin
drugs.mechanismOfAction: An 8-aminoquinoline metabolized into reactive intermediates that generate oxidative stress and disrupt mitochondrial function in hepatic hypnozoites.
drugs.sideEffects: Severe hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency, methemoglobinemia, gastrointestinal upset, leukopenia
drugs.contraindications: G6PD deficiency (must be tested before use), pregnancy, severe rheumatoid arthritis or lupus
drugs.tooltip: The only drug that clears hypnozoites, so it is required to prevent vivax and ovale relapse. G6PD testing before prescribing is mandatory to avoid catastrophic hemolysis.

drugs.name: Ivermectin
drugs.primaryEffect: Paralyzes and kills parasitic nematodes
drugs.treatmentUsage: Strongyloidiasis, onchocerciasis (river blindness), scabies, head lice, cutaneous larva migrans
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds glutamate-gated chloride channels found only in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells, causing hyperpolarization, paralysis, and death of the parasite.
drugs.sideEffects: Dizziness, pruritus, rash, Mazzotti reaction with fever and lymphadenopathy from dying microfilariae, encephalopathy if Loa loa coinfection is present
drugs.contraindications: High Loa loa microfilarial burden because of fatal encephalopathy risk; caution with drugs affecting the blood-brain barrier
drugs.tooltip: Selective because glutamate-gated chloride channels exist only in invertebrates, and P-glycoprotein keeps the drug out of the human brain. Essential before steroids in patients from Strongyloides-endemic areas.

drugs.name: Albendazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Kills helminths by depleting their energy stores
drugs.treatmentUsage: Neurocysticercosis, hydatid disease, pinworm, hookworm, ascariasis, whipworm, giardiasis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds parasite beta-tubulin with high selectivity, preventing microtubule polymerization so glucose uptake fails and the worm depletes its glycogen and ATP.
drugs.sideEffects: Abdominal pain, elevated transaminases, bone marrow suppression with prolonged use, alopecia, teratogenicity; inflammatory reactions when cysticerci die
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy; requires concurrent corticosteroids in neurocysticercosis to blunt inflammation from dying larvae
drugs.tooltip: Selectivity comes from higher affinity for parasite beta-tubulin than human tubulin. In neurocysticercosis, steroids and often antiepileptics are given first because dying cysts trigger severe inflammation and seizures.

drugs.name: Praziquantel
drugs.primaryEffect: Causes paralysis and tegument disruption in flatworms
drugs.treatmentUsage: Schistosomiasis, liver flukes such as Clonorchis, tapeworm infections including Taenia and Diphyllobothrium
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Increases calcium permeability of the parasite tegument, causing sustained muscular contraction, paralysis, and exposure of parasite antigens to host immunity.
drugs.sideEffects: Abdominal pain, dizziness, headache, malaise, fever from dying parasites; seizures if neurocysticercosis is unrecognized
drugs.contraindications: Ocular cysticercosis because parasite destruction damages the eye; concurrent strong CYP inducers reduce levels
drugs.tooltip: The drug of choice for all schistosome species and most flukes and tapeworms. Remember praziquantel for flat worms (trematodes and cestodes), albendazole for round worms (nematodes).

drugs.name: Rifaximin
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces gut bacterial load without systemic absorption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hepatic encephalopathy prevention, traveler's diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Rifamycin derivative that inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; its structure prevents gut absorption so it acts entirely within the intestinal lumen.
drugs.sideEffects: Flatulence, abdominal pain, nausea, peripheral edema; systemic effects are minimal, and Clostridioides difficile risk is low
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to rifamycins
drugs.tooltip: Nearly zero systemic absorption is the entire point. In hepatic encephalopathy it reduces ammonia-producing gut flora and is added to lactulose to prevent recurrence.
